column1: # config/units.tsv -- unit, address, size, state (match: in the gate; open: parked), flag class, source,
# optional entry symbol. A game unit is one original object, or the part of one that the evidence settles.
# Above each game unit, "# premise:" names the joins inside it that rest on the RCS premise alone (every
# object from 0x8000BAA8 on opens its read-only data with an RCS run, which the project accepts: in every
# assignment of the RCS starts to the positions that meets it, no run lies where an object starting there
# would need one). "# open:" names a position between game functions that no evidence settles
# (./wof unitmap: "unknown"), above the unit after it; "# open inside:" one a unit holds on evidence
# unitmap does not read, and which. Every open position was tested with all of: the text padding (a 4-byte
# gap ends an object, a function ending off an 8-byte boundary with the next right after joins one); the
# read-only data (object starts at RCS runs and alignment zeros, bracketed and put in order; contiguous
# items; items in text order; one string literal used on both sides; one string at two addresses); the
# objects' static .bss (shared statics and their order); .data and .bss interleaving between two
# functions' private data; the order of the units' .data against their users; stale fill that ends an
# object's .data; the RCS premise; and the call graph (helpers called from one place, proc handlers named
# by their creator, function addresses in data), which fails at certain positions and so decides
# nothing. The order of the common .bss (uninitialised globals) was compared with the order of their
# first users and does not follow it.
